main.text: [III, 374] Chapter 12. [col. 517]
On honey and wax.

Next we must speak of honey, which Scripture mentions in many places. In Hebrew honey is [col. 518] called דבש debas, an ambiguous name, by which dates are also designated. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon: ונקראו התמרים דבש, They also called dates DEBAS (that is, honey). R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] and the same Kimchi wish it to be taken in this way in 2 Chr 31:6, where the Israelites are said to have offered the first fruits of grain, of must and of oil, ודבש, and of debas, that is, they say, of dates. Kimchi adds that the ancients took it thus in Deut 8:8, in which passage God promises that He will bring him into a land זית שמן ודבש, of oil-bearing olives and of debas. To this point belongs the fact that in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] دبوس [dabūs] dubous are خلاص تمر يلقي في مسلاء السمن فيذوب فيه [khalāṣ tamr yulqā fī maslāʾ al-samn fa-yadhūbu fīhi] choicer dates, which are thrown into melted butter, so as to dissolve in it. And دبس [dibs] dibs, or dibis, is غسل التمر وغسل النخل [ghasl al-tamr wa-ghasl al-nakhl] the honey of the date and the honey of the palm, that is, the juice of the date or of the palm. It rightly shares its name with honey, since its taste is similar. Josephus, The Jewish War, book 5, chapter 3, speaking of the valley of Jericho: It produces most beautiful and very dense gardens, and many kinds of irrigated palms, varying both in taste and in names. Τούτων οἱ πιότεροι πατούμενοι, καὶ μέλι δαψιλὲς ἀνίασιν, οὐ πολλῷ τοῦ λοιποῦ χεῖρον· [Toutōn hoi pioteroi patoumenoi, kai meli dapsiles aniasin, ou pollō tou loipou cheiron] The richest of these, when trodden, give out a great deal of honey, not much inferior to other honey. And another Josephus, closer in time indeed but more remote in place, namely the Indian, in his Voyage, chapter 138: In the month of August the Indians prune the palm. And since the trees are then at their most luxuriant, when cut they groan, and emit tears like a wounded vine. These they catch in vessels for only three days after the tree has been wounded, etc. But whoever wishes to make sugar, let him take water of this kind flowing out within three days, and put it in copper pots and boil it, until scarcely a third part remains. Then, thus boiled down, it becomes a most sweet honey. It is therefore clear why the Hebrews gave the name of honey either to dates or to the juice of the palm ^{R1}. Indeed R. Selomo on Lev 2:11 extends it much more widely, as though דבש debas meant כל מתיקת פרי, all sweetness of fruit ^{R2}. However that may be, here we are dealing with honey properly so called.

[III, 375] Of this there are two kinds: one domestic, from bees that are kept at home; the other wild, such as John is said to have lived on in the desert, Matt 3:4. His food was locusts and wild honey. And Mark 1:6. Eating locusts and wild honey. Since the two Evangelists expressly write μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion], wild honey, it is surprising that there are some who understand μελαγρίαν [melagrian] as a kind of plant which, if we believe them, grows in the desert. Suidas: Μελαγρία· εἶδος βοτάνης φυομένης ἐν ἐρήμῳ [Melagria; eidos botanēs phyomenēs en erēmō]. Others write τὰ μέλαγρα [ta melagra], as though there were a plant of this name, which they otherwise call ἀκρίδας [akridas]. Theophylact: Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι [Tines legousi botanas einai tas akridas, has kai melagra kalousi]; Some say that the acrides are plants, which they also call melagra. Even if we granted this, it would still be beside the point. For we do not read that John ate μελαγρίαν [melagrian] or μέλαγρα [melagra], but μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. No more acceptable is what Bede in his book De locis sanctis, and Thomas on Matthew, report from Arnulphus or Archulphus: that in the desert of John there were trees with broad, round leaves, of milky colour and honeyed taste, which, being naturally brittle, are rubbed in the hands and eaten, and that this is called wild honey. [col. 519] Nor do I agree with Christianus Druthmarus, for whom the wild honey in this passage is that very Manna on which the children of Israel were fed for forty years. The taste of Manna was indeed כצפיחת בדבש, like the taste of a honeyed wafer, Exod 16:31. And accordingly Manna is called by some δροσόμελι [drosomeli] and ἀερόμελι [aeromeli] ^{R3}. Yet Manna is one thing, wild [III, 376] honey another. Nor should new meanings be foisted onto the words of Scripture when the received ones can fit. Here, therefore, I understand nothing other than locusts and wild honey. And we have already shown ^{a)} that locusts are frequent in those regions and therefore were accepted as food. The same about wild honey is easy to prove from Scripture itself. Well known is the saying of Solomon, Prov 25:16: Have you found honey? Eat as much as is sufficient. And this doubtless refers to wild honey, which was found here and there in the fields. Thus when Samson had come upon a lion in the field and torn it apart, [III, 377] in the following year he found honey which bees had produced in its carcass, Iud. XIV, 8. Of the same kind is what we read in 1 Sam. XIV, 25. 26: The people came into the forest, in which there was honey על פני השדה, on the surface of the field. And the people entered that forest, and behold הלך דבש, a flow of honey. This, namely, was wild honey, which bees had made either on the bare ground, or in hollow trees, or in clefts of rocks. Such a rock is called in Hebrew צור דבש, rock of honey, Ps 81:17. And the honey flowing from it is דבש מסלע, honey from the rock, Deut 32:13. So from the word יער jaar, which means forest (as jar in Punic means wood according to Augustine on Psalm 23), יער jaar, or יערה jaara, is a honeycomb, properly one found in the forest. As in 1 Sam. XIV, 27: Jonathan stretched out the tip of the rod that he had in his hand, and dipped it ביערת הדבש, in the honeycomb. And Cant. V, 1: I have eaten יערי, my honeycomb with my honey ^{R4}. Nor is there reason for anyone to believe that it was peculiar to Judaea that bees made honey here and there in fields or forests. For we have already learned ^{b)} the same of Scythia and Muscovy from reliable writers. And Maldonatus on Matthew reports that he saw poor men in Baetica who gathered honey from the forests and made their living by selling it. Accordingly the poets frequently mention bees [III, 378] that nest in hollow trees, in reed-beds, or in caves. Hesiod, Theogony, line 230:
— — — οὔρεσι δὲ δρῦς Ἄκρη μέν τε φέρει βαλάνους, μέσση δὲ μελίσσας, [ouresi de drys / akrē men te pherei balanous, messē de melissas,]

On the mountains the oak bears acorns at its top, and bees in its middle. That is, ἐν τοῖς κοιλώμασι τῶν στελέχων [en tois koilōmasi tōn stelechōn], in the hollows of the trunks, as the Scholiast there explains. Phocylides, or whoever he is, in the Νουθετικῷ [Nouthetikō], line 160:

Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος, ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα, Ἠὲ πέτρης κοίλης κατὰ χηραμὸν, ἢ δονάκεσσιν, Ἢ δρυὸς ὠγυγίης κατὰ κοιλάδος· [Kamnei d' ēerophoitos, aristoponos te melissa, / Ēe petrēs koilēs kata chēramon, ē donakessin, / Ē dryos ōgygiēs kata koilados;]
The air-roaming and hard-working bee also labours, either in the cave of a hollow rock, or among reeds, or in the hollow of an ancient oak. Virgil, Georgics, book 4 [vv. 43 ff.]:
Often too (if the report is true) they have made their home in hollows dug beneath the earth, and have been found deep within porous rocks and in the cavity of a hollowed tree.
Statius, Thebaid, book 10, line 569:
So when a shepherd, about to plunder, has driven the armed bees from their pumice cave. — — —
Claudian, De raptu, book 2:
— — and, sent forth from the hollow belly of a beech, the honey-bearing army hums over the chosen herbs.

Moreover, according to the Philosopher, History book 5, chapter 22, Αἱ δ' ἐν Θεμισκύρᾳ περὶ τὸν Θερμώδοντα ποταμὸν, ἐν τῇ γῇ, καὶ ἐν τοῖς σμήνεσι ποιοῦντες κηρία· [Hai d' en Themiskyra peri ton Thermōdonta potamon, en tē gē, kai en tois smēnesi poiountes kēria] At Themiscyra, near the river Thermodon, they make honeycombs both in the ground and in hives. And further on: Κατάγεται δὲ καὶ εἰς Ἀμισὸν ἄνωθεν μέλι λευκὸν, καὶ παχὺ σφόδρα, ὃ ποιοῦσιν αἱ μέλιτται ἄνευ κηρίων πρὸς τοῖς δένδρεσι, γίνεται δὲ τοιοῦτον καὶ ἄλλοθι ἐν τῷ Πόντῳ. [Katagetai de kai eis Amison anōthen meli leukon, kai pachy sphodra, ho poiousin hai melittai aneu kēriōn pros tois dendresi, ginetai de toiouton kai allothi en tō Pontō.] To the city of Amisus [col. 520] white and very thick honey is brought down from the higher regions, which the bees make on trees without honeycombs. Honey of this kind is also produced in other places of Pontus. Likewise: Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ μέλιτται, αἳ ποιοῦσι τριπλᾶ κηρία ἐν τῇ γῇ· [Eisi de kai melittai, hai poiousi tripla kēria en tē gē] There are also bees which make honeycombs in a triple row on the ground ^{R5}. Thus wild honey can be found elsewhere too; but more frequently in Judaea ^{R6}, [III, 379] which is called more than once ^{c)} a land of oil and honey, and in about twenty places ^{d)} a land flowing with milk and honey, that is, most fertile in the produce of milk and honey. The phrase is also common among the poets: Euripides in the Bacchae, verse 142:
Ῥεῖ δὲ γάλακτι πέδον, Ῥεῖ δ’ οἴνῳ, ῥεῖ δὲ μελισσῶν Νέκταρι· — — — [Rhei de galakti pedon, Rhei d' oinō, rhei de melissōn Nektari]
The field flows with milk, it flows also with wine, it flows with the nectar of bees. Virgil, Eclogue 3:
May honey flow for him, and may the rough bramble bear amomum.
Ovid, Metamorphoses book 1, on the golden age:
Now rivers of milk, now rivers of nectar flowed.
Nectar, that is, honey, as above in Euripides. Horace, book 2, Ode 19:
— — to sing of rich streams of milk, and to tell again of honey dripping from hollow trunks.
Claudian, In Praise of Stilicho book 1, verse 84:
[III, 380] Then, they say, the horses of the sun and the stars leapt in dances, and lakes of honey and rivers of milk burst forth from the ground. — — — —

Such is the mention in Iob. XX, 17 of נחלי דבש וחמאה, torrents of honey and butter. This expression is hyperbolic in such a way that it partly suits honey, because honey flows down from the comb when it is abundant. This flowing of honey is expressed in various ways among the Hebrews and Syrians. First by the word הלך halach, which properly means to go or to walk. But in 1 Sam 14:26, הלך דבש is a flow of honey. So in Ovid above:
— — now rivers of nectar went [flowed],

that is, they were flowing. Second, by the name נופת nopheth, which means distillation, since נוף nuph is a verb meaning to drip or to sprinkle. Thus in Ps 19:11. נופת צופים is the distillation of honeycombs. And in Song 4:11. נופת תטפנה, Your lips drip distillation. And in Prov 5:3. The lips of a harlot drip distillation. So also Prov 24:13. ונופת, And distillation is sweet to your palate. And Prov 27:7. The sated soul tramples נופת, the dripping, supply of honey or of honeycombs. For this is to be supplied everywhere. Third, from the verb צוף, that is, to flow, צוף tsuph is the name of a honeycomb, properly a flowing one. Thus Prov 16:24. צוף דבש, pleasant words are a honeycomb (a flowing one). And Ps 19:11. The judgments of the Lord are sweeter than honey, ונופת צופים, and than the distillation of honeycombs (flowing ones). Fourth, the verb רדה rada, which the Hebrews render to take, the Syrians in Iud. XIV, 9., following the idiom of their own language, refer to the flowing of honey, because for them ܢܕܼ [נד] means to flow. So these words about the honey found by Samson, וירדהו אל כפיו, And he took it into his hands, are rendered thus by the Syriac translator: ܘܢܕܼ ܗܘܐ ܕܒܫܐ ܥܠ ܐܝܕܘܗܝ ܘܡܗܠܟ [ונד הוא דבשא על אידוהי ומהלך] And the honey flowed down over his hands, and he went on. And again in the same verse, He did not tell them that he had רדה הדבש, taken the honey, from the body of the lion. So the Hebrews; but the Syrians have ܢܕܼ ܕܒܫܐ [נד דבשא], the honey had flowed: as in 1 Sam 14:25 (or 26.) ܘܢܕܼ ܗܘܐ ܕܒܫܐ [ונד הוא דבשא] And that honey was flowing. Fifth, in the same place the flowing of honey is, in the Chaldee, בריז דובשא. For برز [baraza] baraza in Arabic is to go out. Hence בריז brez, or briz, in Chaldee is the flow of honey going out from the comb. To this perhaps belongs the fact that the inventor of honey, Bacchus, was called Brisaeus or Bressaeus. Cornutus on Persius, Satire 1: Father Liber is surnamed BRISAEUS from the use of honey, because he himself is said to have first discovered honey and to press it from the combs (read to have pressed). Hesychius: Βρησσαῖος· Διόνυσος [Brēssaios; Dionysos]. To the same point is the fact that they called Brisae the Nymphs who taught Aristaeus [col. 521] the method of making honey. Heraclides in the Constitution of the Coans, or rather of the Ceans: Ἀρισταῖον δέ φασι μαθεῖν παρὰ Βρισσῶν τὴν μελιττουργίαν [Aristaion de phasi mathein para Brissōn tēn melittourgian]. The Etymologicum: Βρίσαι· Νύμφαι οὕτω καλουμέναι [Brisai; Nymphai houtō kaloumenai]. And immediately after: Μελιττουργίαν αὐταὶ τὸν Ἀρισταῖον ἐδίδαξαν [Melittourgian autai ton Aristaion edidaxan].

[III, 381] It has been proved so far that honey abounded in Judaea and was produced plentifully, even in the fields and woods. Why, then, could it not have been used as food by John the Baptist? To many, ordinary honey seems too luxurious a food to have suited John in such abstinence. Accordingly they hold that the wild honey of which the Evangelists speak was bitter and altogether unpleasant to the taste. Thus Isidore of Pelusium, Epistle 132, defines it as μέλι ὄρειον, ὑπὸ μελισσῶν ἀγρίων γινόμενον, πικρότατον, καὶ πάσῃ γεύσει πολέμιον [meli oreion, hypo melissōn agriōn ginomenon, pikrotaton, kai pasē geusei polemion]. And Euthymius says: Wild honey is made by wild bees in the clefts of rocks; but it is bitter and unpleasant. But these things are said without grounds, and do not agree well with Scripture, which would not so greatly commend Judaea for its honey if the honey produced in the fields were unpleasant and bitter. I am not unaware that in certain places bitter honey is produced, for example the Sardinian and the Corsican, whether the cause lies in the wormwood on which the bees feed (Dioscorides, book 2: Τὸ δὲ ἐν Σαρδονίᾳ γενώμενον μέλι πικρὸν διὰ τὴν τοῦ ἀψινθίου νομήν [To de en Sardonia genōmenon meli pikron dia tēn tou apsinthiou nomēn]; Galen, On the Simple Faculty of Medicines, book 7: If any honey is bitter, as the Sardinian, it is clear that it too is of a mixed faculty, as if one of us had mixed wormwood into it); or whether it comes from the box tree, which is very abundant in Corsica (Diodorus, book 5: Φύεται δὲ κατὰ τὴν νῆσον ταύτην καὶ πύξος πλείστη, καὶ διάφορος· δι’ ἣν καὶ τὸ μέλι τὸ γινόμενον ἐν αὐτῇ παντελῶς γίνεται πικρόν [Phyetai de kata tēn nēson tautēn kai pyxos pleistē, kai diaphoros; di’ hēn kai to meli to ginomenon en autē pantelōs ginetai pikron]); or from yews, as these lines of the poet suggest, in Eclogue 5:
So may your swarms shun the Cyrnean yews.

On which Servius: The yew is a poisonous tree, which abounds in Corsica. Likewise: Cyrenean yews, fed on which bees make a most bitter honey. Or from feeding on hemlock, as Ovid writes of wax in the Amores, book 1, Elegy 12:
Which, I think, the Corsican bee sent, gathered from afar from the hemlock flower, under infamous honey.
Or from thyme of bad flavour, as Martial, book 11, Epigram 13:
You bid Hyblaean or Hymettian honey to be born for you, and you set Corsican thyme before the Cecropian bee.

Elsewhere too there is poisonous honey, which drives those who eat it to madness. Such is the honey around Heraclea Pontica, of which Dioscorides ^{e)} and Pliny ^{f)} speak; and that near Trapezus, of which Aristotle ^{g)} and Aelian ^{h)} speak. Many others also mention it, but Xenophon ^{i)} and Diodorus Siculus ^{k)} place it among the Colchians, Strabo ^{l)} among the Heptacometae, and Pliny among the [III, 382] Sanni ^{m)}). From the same author I have learned that poisonous honeycombs are produced also in Persia, and in the Gaetulia of Mauretania Caesariensis bordering on the Massaesylii ^{R7}. But that bitter honey, or honey in any way defective, is produced in Judaea has never been heard of even in a dream. Indeed in Gen 43:11 honey is among the מזמרת ארץ, the things praised and celebrated in the land of Canaan ^{R8}. And the blasphemer Rabshakeh commends Assyria on the ground that, like the land of Canaan, it is fruitful in olives and honey, 2 Reg. XVIII, 32. So in Josephus, book 5 On the War, ch. 4, one of the praises of the territory of Jericho is that it is μελιττοτρόφος ἡ χώρα [melittotrophos hē chōra], a region suited to the rearing of bees. And Alcamus mentions among choice things the Thecoan honey, named after the town of Tekoa, near Jerusalem. His words are: تقوع بالقدس ينسب اليه العسل [Taqūʿ bi-l-Quds yunsabu ilayhi al-ʿasal] Tekoa, a town near Kuds (that is, Jerusalem), after which honey is named, or else whose honey is renowned. Accordingly honey was exported from Judaea to other lands: to the markets of the Tyrians, Ezek 27:17 and to Egypt, Gen 43:11. Although we also read that Egypt itself abounded in honey, Num 16:13. Nor should anyone imagine that these things are said only of domestic honey. [col. 522] For wild was the honey whose sweetness Samson extolled in such splendid words, Iud. XIV, 14. And so was that other honey, on tasting which Jonathan's eyes were opened, 1 Sam. 14. 29. Wild also was the honey of the rock, that is, honey flowing from the clefts of rocks in which wild bees made their honey. Yet it is counted among the delights that God offered to his people, Deut 32:13 He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the produce of the fields, and he gave him honey to suck from the rock. Ps 81:17 He will feed him with the fat of wheat, and with honey from the rock he will satisfy him. Thus both in wild [III, 383] and in domestic honey there was what pleased the palate. Yet in John the Baptist it was a mark of great abstinence that he lived on locusts and wild honey alone: because, as in locusts (as was proved in its place), so also in honey there is little nourishment when it is taken alone and by itself. Hippocrates, ch. 50 On Affections: Τὸ μέλι, ξὺν ἑτέροις ἐσθιόμενον, καὶ τρέφει· καὶ εὔχροιαν παρέχει. Αὐτὸ δὲ ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτῷ λεπτύνει μᾶλλον, ἢ κομίζει [To meli, xyn heterois esthiomenon, kai trephei; kai euchroian parechei. Auto de eph᾽ heautō leptynei mallon, ē komizei], Honey, eaten with other things, both nourishes and gives a good colour. But by itself it rather thins than restores. The ancients celebrate the abstinence of Aristoxenus, the Cyrenaic philosopher, on the ground that θρίδακα ἐν κήπῳ οἰνομέλιτι ποτίζων ἑσπέρας, καὶ ὑπὸ τὴν ἕω λαμβάνων, χλωροὺς ἔχειν ἔλεγε πλακοῦντας [thridaka en kēpō oinomeliti potizōn hesperas, kai hypo tēn heō lambanōn, chlōrous echein elege plakountas], watering lettuce in his garden with honeyed wine towards evening and taking it in the morning, he said he had yellow cakes. And that of Pythagoras, because εὐτελέστατα διαβιοὺς, πολλάκις μέλιτι μόνῳ ἠρκεῖτο [eutelestata diabious, pollakis meliti monō ērkeito], he lived so frugally that he was often content with honey alone. So Eustathius reports on Iliad λ΄ [11]. But our John far surpasses both. For Aristoxenus added wine and lettuce to the honey, from which John abstained. And Pythagoras was content with honey alone often, yet not always. For Laertius says of him: Ἐνίοτε δὲ αὐτὸν ἀρκεῖσθαι μέλιτι μόνῳ φασί τινες, ἢ κηρίῳ, ἢ ἄρτῳ· οἴνου δὲ μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν μὴ γεύσασθαι· ὄψον τε τὰ πολλὰ λαχάνοις ἑφθοῖς, καὶ ὠμοῖς, τοῖς δὲ θαλαττίοις σπανίως [Eniote de auton arkeisthai meliti monō phasi tines, ē kēriō, ē artō; oinou de meth᾽ hēmeran mē geusasthai; opson te ta polla lachanois hephthois, kai ōmois, tois de thalattiois spaniōs]. Some say that he sometimes lived content with honey alone, or a honeycomb, or bread; but that during the day (that is, until evening) he did not taste wine; and that for relish he mostly had boiled or raw vegetables, and seldom used seafood. Moreover, these men ate purchased food, whereas John fed on whatever chance offered, relying so firmly on God's providence that in the desert he depended on it alone, certain that the things necessary to sustain life would not fail him.

Honey is commended above all for the sweetness of its taste. Hence the Son of Sirach, above, on the bee: Ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς [Archē glykasmatōn ho karpos autēs], The beginning of sweet things (or, is supremely sweet) is its fruit. And Samson, in the riddle he put to the Philistines at the wedding feast, Iud. XIV, 14. Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness: that is, honey out of the lion. For we have already learned that honey was found in the body of the lion. The Hebrew has בגוית האריה, the Greek Ἐν ςόματι τοῦ λέοντος [En stomati tou leontos]; but this should be corrected to ἐν σώματι [en sōmati]. Likewise in verse 9, where the Complutensian edition and the recent Paris edition read Ἐκ τῆς ἕξεως τοῦ λέοντος ἐξεῖλεν τὸ μέλι [Ek tēs hexeōs tou leontos exeilen to meli], I would restore ἐκ τῆς ἰξύος [ek tēs ixyos], from the loin, as the rendering of גויה, since גו is commonly taken for the back or rear, where the loins are. But the less frequent word ἰξύος [ixyos] was changed into ἕξεως [hexeōs] through the ignorance of scribes, whose habit it is to corrupt whatever they do not understand. However that may be, since Samson had taken honey out of a lion's body, a thing otherwise without precedent, he drew from it the subject of a griphus or riddle. For it was the custom among the ancients to propose questions at banquets, in the solving of which their wits were exercised. [III, 384] Clearchus calls such a question a griphus, and in Athenaeus defines it thus: Γρίφος πρόβλημά ἐστι παιστικὸν, προστακτικὸν τοῦ διὰ ζητήσεως εὑρεῖν τῇ διανοίᾳ τὸ προβληθὲν, τιμῆς ἢ ἐπιζημίου χάριν εἰρημένον [Griphos problēma esti paistikon, prostaktikon tou dia zētēseōs heurein tē dianoia to problēthen, timēs ē epizēmiou charin eirēmenon]. A griphus is a playful problem, by which one is bidden to find out by searching of the mind what has been proposed, put forward for the sake of a reward or a penalty. And that such were customarily proposed to guests at table, Athenaeus shows at length in book 10. Julius [col. 523] Pollux also mentions them in book 6, chapter 19, where he distinguishes the riddles and griphi of drinking companions, holding that the former were always jocular, the latter sometimes serious. His words are: Τῶν μὲν συμποτικῶν αἴνιγμα καὶ γρῖφος· τὸ μὲν παιδιὰν εἶχεν, ὁ δὲ γρῖφος καὶ σπουδήν [Tōn men sympotikōn ainigma kai griphos; to men paidian eichen, ho de griphos kai spoudēn]. He goes on to say that the one who solved it was given a dish of meat, κρεῶν τινα περιφορὰν [kreōn tina periphoran], just as ἅλμης ποτήριον [halmēs potērion], a cup of brine, was given to be drunk by the one who could not solve it. Other rewards too, and likewise other penalties, customary among the Greeks, may be read in Athenaeus in the place cited. Gellius, book 18, ch. 2, reports that something of the sort was practised by Romans at Athens during the Saturnalia: Several of us Romans who had come to Greece and attended the same lectures and the same teachers used to meet at the same dinner. Then the one whose turn it was to provide the little dinner would set as the prize for solving a question a book by an old writer, either Greek or Latin, and a crown woven of laurel; and he would ask as many questions as there were men present. When he had set them all out, the lot assigned the question and the order of speaking. If the question was solved, the man was presented with the crown and the prize; if it was not solved, it passed to the one who came next by lot. And this was kept up in turn around the circle. If no one untied the knot of the question, the prize itself and the crown were dedicated to the god whose festival it was. But nothing establishes the antiquity of the custom so much as what we read of Samson: that he proposed to his thirty guests a riddle to be solved within the seven days of the feast, on the condition that, if they solved it, they would receive as a prize thirty linen garments and as many changes of clothing; if not, they themselves would give them. The riddle was this: Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. In these words, as food is set against the eater, so sweetness is set against the strong. Yet these do not seem to be opposites. For the opposite of strong is unwarlike or weak; the opposite of sweet is sharp or bitter. But sometimes these are confused, and bitter is taken for strong, and sharp for both. Thus in Arabic مرة [mirra] mirra, that is, strength, and مرير [marīr] merir, that is, robust, vigorous, come from the verb مر [marra] marra, which means to be bitter. And in Latin a man who is strong is called acer [sharp], as in Aeneid book 8:
Or would you hesitate to call bold Turnus to battle?

On which passage Servius says: ACREM TURNUM) strong. And properly with us acer is what δεινὸς [deinos] is among the Greeks. For it can mean strong, and vehement, and harsh, and bitter. Nonius likewise: Acrem, strong, Aen. book 7 (read book 8). Rightly therefore Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] at Judg 14:14: From the sharp came forth sweetness. And in the solution of [III, 385] the riddle, verse 18: What is sweeter than honey? And what is sharper than a lion? As in book 4 of the Fasti:
— — — the fierce race of lions.

Further, because honey is not only sweet but also ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων [archē glykasmatōn], it follows that whatever is either sweet to the taste or pleasing and delightful to the mind is compared with honey. Thus it is said of the Manna in Exod 16:31. And its taste was כצפיחת בדבש, like cakes with honey, that is, honeyed. For the food was so sweet that the author of Wisdom seems to regard it as a kind of ambrosia, when he calls it εὔτηκτον γένος ἀμβροσίας τροφῆς [eutēkton genos ambrosias trophēs], ch. 19, 20. By this very name honey is called by an ancient Poet,
— — — ἡ δὲ μελισσῶν Ἀμβροσίη, πυκναί τ' ἰτρίνεαι ποπάδες· [hē de melissōn Ambrosiē, pyknai t' itrineai popades]

The ambrosia of bees, and many very thin cakes. So Suidas quotes it under Ποπάδες [Popades]. And the Prophetic scroll was to Ezekiel and John sweeter than honey, Ezek 3:3. Rev 10:9–10. So too the commandments of the Lord, of which David says, Ps 19:11: They are sweeter than honey and the dripping of honeycombs. And Ps 119:103: How sweet have your words been to my palate, more than honey to my mouth. Likewise divine wisdom, Prov 24:13–14: My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the honeycomb, which is sweet to your palate. So shall the knowledge of wisdom (be sweet) to your soul, if you find it, [col. 524] etc. And Sir 24:19–20. (var. 26. 27.) Wisdom herself says: Come to me, you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits: for the remembrance of me is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance than the honeycomb. In Greek, Ὑπὲρ μέλιτος κηροῦ [Hyper melitos kērou]; others read κυροῦ [kyrou], others κληροῦ [klērou], others κηρίου [kēriou], others κυρίου [kyriou]. Perhaps the author had written in one word μελικήρου [melikērou], for μελίκηρος [melikēros] is a honeycomb. The word is not found in the Lexicons, but it is read in Theocritus, Idyll. 20.
— — — ἐκ στομάτων δὲ Ἔῤῥεέ μοι φωνὰ γλυκερωτέρα, ἢ μελικήρῳ· [ek stomatōn de Errhee moi phōna glykerōtera, ē melikērō]

And from my mouth flowed a voice sweeter than the honeycomb. From there the Son of Sirach could have taken it, for he wrote a few years after Theocritus, and both in Egypt. This conjecture is supported by the Syriac and Arabic versions, for both have simply honeycomb here, not honeycomb of honey. But Jerome has honey and honeycomb. In the same book, ch. 49, 2, the memory or mention of Josiah ἐν παντὶ στόματι ὡς μέλι γλυκανθήσεται [en panti stomati hōs meli glykanthēsetai], will be sweet as honey in every mouth. And of the bridegroom we read in the Chaldee paraphrast, Song 5:6. מלי מוריגוי מתוקן כרבשא, The words of his palate are sweet as honey; for the Hebrew חכו ממתקים, His palate is sweetnesses. And of the bride, Song 4:11: Your lips drip the honeycomb, honey and milk are under your tongue. So the poet says of Nestor, Iliad α, line 249:
[III, 386] Τοῦ καὶ ἀπὸ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίον ῥεὲν αὐδής, [Tou kai apo glōssēs melitos glykion rheen audēs]
From whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey. And Theocritus, Idyll. 8:
Κρεῖσσον μελπομένῳ τεῦ ἀκουέμεν, ἢ μέλι λείχειν. [Kreisson melpomenō teu akouemen, ē meli leichein.]
It is better to hear you singing than to lick honey. And Moschus of Love, Idyll. 1:
— — — ὡς μέλι φωνὰ, [hōs meli phōna]

His voice (is sweet) as honey ^{R9}. Which Solomon says of the harlot, Prov 5:3: The lips of the strange woman drip the honeycomb. And Statius of Glaucias in the Epicedium, book 2 of the Silvae, [III, 387] — — — and deep within, as he spoke, his voice was mingled with Hyblaean honeycombs. — —

Hence throughout Pindar ^{n)} μελιγάρυες ὕμνοι [meligaryes hymnoi], and ^{o)} μελίφθογγοι ἀοιδαί [meliphthongoi aoidai]. And, in Illustrius, Sophocles, the tragedian, μέλιττα ἐκαλεῖτο διὰ τὸ ἡδὺ [melitta ekaleito dia to hēdy], was called a bee because of the sweetness of his verse: as Xenophon in Suidas is Ἀττικὴ μέλιττα [Attikē melitta], the Attic bee. And in Aristophanes' Birds,
— — ὥσπερ ἡ μέλιττα Φρύνιχος ἀμβροσίων Μελέων ἀπεβόσκετο καρπὸν ἀεὶ, Φέρων γλυκεῖαν ᾠδάν· [hōsper hē melitta Phrynichos ambrosiōn Meleōn apebosketo karpon aei, Pherōn glykeian ōdan]
Like a bee, Phrynichus (the comic poet) always fed on the fruit of ambrosial songs, bringing a sweet song. And in Anthology book 5, on a statue of Sappho,
Πιερικὴ δὲ μέλιττα λιγύθροος ἕζετο Σαπφὼ, [Pierikē de melitta ligythroos hezeto Sapphō]
And there sat the sweet-sounding Pierian bee, Sappho. And on Erinna,
Πιερικῆς ῥαθάμιγγας ἀποσταλάουσα μελίσσης, [Pierikēs rhathamingas apostalaousa melissēs]
Dripping the drops of the Pierian bee. And on Homer,
Πιερικὴ δὲ μέλισσα περὶ στόμα θεῖον ἀλᾶτο, Κηρίον ὠδίνουσα μελισταγές· — — [Pierikē de melissa peri stoma theion alato, Kērion ōdinousa melistages]

And the Pierian bee wandered about his divine mouth, bringing forth a honeycomb dripping with honey. To the same point belongs what Pliny ^{p)} and others ^{q)} report, that bees settled on the mouth of the infant Plato, foretelling the charm of his exceedingly sweet eloquence. Authors not to be despised write the same of Pindar ^{r)}, Lucan ^{s)} and Ambrose ^{t)}.

The ancient Hebrews placed honey among the things most necessary for life. Thus Sir 39:31 Ἀρχὴ πάσης χρείας εἰς ζωὴν ἀνθρώπου, ὕδωρ, πῦρ, καὶ σίδηρος, καὶ ἅλας, καὶ σεμίδαλις πυροῦ, καὶ μέλι, etc. [Archē pasēs chreias eis zōēn anthrōpou, hydōr, pyr, kai sidēros, kai halas, kai semidalis pyrou, kai meli] The principal things of every necessity for the life of man (that is, they hold first place among the things most required for life) are water, fire, iron, salt, grain, fine flour, honey, etc. For honey was useful for many purposes: for food, for drink, for medicine, for [col. 525] preserving corpses. Finally, superstitious people used honey in their rites. As for the eating of honey, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] in his Paraphrase on Lev 11:20 says of it: The kinds [III, 388] of bees shall be an abomination to you. Yet דובשא דזיבורי יתאכל, the honey of bees shall be eaten. The Arabs write the same thing, and illustrate it by the example of human milk, the drinking of which is permitted, although human flesh is forbidden. Accordingly the eating of honey is dealt with here and there in Scripture. Thus Deuter. XXXII, 13. He gave him honey to suck from the rock. Ps 81:17 With honey from the rock I will satisfy you. Prov 24:13 My son, eat honey, because it is good. Prov 25:16 When you find honey, eat as much as is sufficient for you. Isa 7:22 Whoever is left in the land shall eat butter and honey. Ezek 16:13 You ate fine flour and honey and oil. Examples are Samson, Judg 14:9; Jonathan, 1 Sam 14:27; Solomon, Song 5:1; John, Matt 3:4; and finally Christ himself, Luke 24:42–43. That this food also suits infancy is proved from the celebrated passage of Isaiah about Emmanuel, ch. VII, 15: He shall eat butter and honey, until he knows to refuse evil and choose good: that is, until he is a little older. Basil: Παιδικῇ τροφῇ χρῆται ὁ Ἐμμανουὴλ διὰ τὴν σάρκα, βουτύρῳ, καὶ μέλιτι· [Paidikē trophē chrētai ho Emmanouēl dia tēn sarka, boutyrō, kai meliti] Because of the flesh Emmanuel uses a child's food, namely butter and honey. Cyril: Τροφὴν αὐτῷ γεγεννῆσθαι λέγων τὴν νηπίοις πρέπουσαν, βούτηρόν τε, καὶ μέλι· [Trophēn autō gegennēsthai legōn tēn nēpiois prepousan, boutēron te, kai meli] Saying that his food would be what suits little children, butter and honey. Jerome: He uses the foods of infancy, „He shall eat butter and honey.“ Bernard [=Bernard of Clairvaux], On Advent, Sermon 2: „He shall eat butter, he says, and milk: as if he were saying, He will be a little child, and will feed on infant foods.“ Hence the ancients gave milk and honey to be tasted beforehand at baptism, in which the faithful are reborn. Tertullian, De corona militis ch. 3: Then, having been taken up, we first taste the concord of milk and honey. Alluding to this, Jerome, against the Luciferians, chapter 4, says that those who have come out of the font first taste the concord of milk and honey as a sign of infancy. For infants were then fed not on milk alone but also on honey. Thus Didymus relates from the most ancient histories of the Cretans that Melisseus, king of the Cretans, had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who nourished the boy Jupiter with goat's milk and honey. So it is found in Lactantius, book 1, On False Religion, ch. 22. And in Antoninus Liberalis, Boeus mentions a cave occupied by ἱεραὶ μέλιτται τροφοὶ τοῦ Διὸς [hierai melittai trophoi tou Dios], sacred bees, nurses of Jupiter. Of the same kind is the story that Πινδάρῳ, τῆς πατρῴας οἰκίας ἐκτεθέντι, μέλιτται τροφοὶ ἐγένοντο ὑπὲρ τοῦ γάλακτος παρατεθεῖσαι μέλι [Pindarō, tēs patrōas oikias ektethenti, melittai trophoi egenonto hyper tou galaktos paratetheisai meli]: for Pindar, driven from his father's house and exposed, bees took the place of nurses, offering him honey instead of milk. Accordingly, if children who were ill had to drink something bitter, the rim of the cup was first smeared with honey, so that they would think their usual food was being offered them. Lucretius:

But as physicians, when they try to give children loathsome wormwood, first touch the rims around the cups with the sweet golden liquid of honey, so that the unsuspecting age of children may be deceived. [III, 389] But although honey is a pleasant food and suits any age, one must nevertheless take care not to overdo it. Hence Solomon, Proverb. XXV, 16: When you find honey, eat as much as is enough for you, lest being sated you vomit it up. And Prov 27:7: The sated soul tramples on the honeycomb. As Pindar, Nemean 7:
Κόρον δ᾽ ἔχει, καὶ μέλι. [Koron d' echei, kai meli.]
Even of honey there is satiety. And an old Epigram:
— — καὶ μέλιτος τὸ πλέον ἐστὶ χόλη, [kai melitos to pleon esti cholē]
Even of honey, what is in excess is gall. A rabbinic proverb also belongs here: אוכל דבש הרבה סופו מקיאה, He who eats much honey vomits it up in the end.

The use of honey in drink seems to be commended by these words of Nehemiah in Jerome's version [col. 526], ch. VIII, 10: Go, eat the fat, and drink mead. So it reads in Jerome. Mulsum [mead], however, is οἰνόμελι [oinomeli], that is, a drink made from wine and honey. The method of preparing it is accurately taught by Dioscorides, book 5, ch. 8, Palladius, book 11, ch. 17, and the authors of the Geoponica, book 8, ch. 25; Pliny also mentions it in passing, book 22, ch. 24. Nor did it escape the Talmudists in the tractate On Idolatry, ch. 2, fol. 30a, where, to the question what אינומלין, οἰνόμελι [oinomeli], is, they answer that it is יין ודבש ופלפלין, wine, and honey, and pepper, mixed and blended together. This description, however, rather belongs to conditum [spiced wine]. Finally, Macrobius, Saturnalia book 7, ch. 12, asks why mead is best blended from fresh honey and old wine. Mead is also frequently mentioned in the poets. Plautus in the Persa, Scene 3:
Mix the mead, get ready quinces and pears.
And in the Stichus, Act 2, Scene 1:
How many draughts of mead, and how many luncheons?
Horace, book 2, Satire 2:
Spurn cheap food, unless you drink Hymettian honey diluted with Falernian. — — —
And Satire 4:
Aufidius used to mix honey with strong Falernian, wrongly; for to empty veins one should commit nothing but what is mild: you will do better to wash your insides with mild mead. — — —
Virgil, book 4 of the Georgics, [III, 390] You will press sweet honey, not so much sweet as clear, and fit to tame the harsh taste of Bacchus.
That is, suited for mead (says Servius), because our ancestors tempered very harsh wines with the sweetness of honey. Martial, book 4, Epigram 13:
As well as rare cinnamon mixes with its ^{u)} nard, so well do Massic wines mix with Thesean honeycombs.
And book 13, Epigram 108:
You muddy nectar-like Falernian with Attic honey; such a drink deserves to be mixed by Ganymede.
Corippus, book 3:
They poured dark Risattic wines into the tawny metal, wines which nature prepares with no need of liquid honey.
They hold that Homer led the way, Iliad κ' [kappa], line 234, where Circe
— — — μέλι χλωρὸν Οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ ἐκύκα, — — [meli chlōron / Oinō Pramneiō ekyka]

mixed fresh honey with Pramnian wine. Indeed, long before Circe, Aristaeus (they say) was the first of all to mix honey with wine. So Pliny, book 14, ch. 4. Yet Plutarch counts οἰνόμελι [oinomeli], mead, among things recently invented. The passage is Table Talk, book 8, Question 9: Πολλὰ γὰρ τῶν ἀγεύστων καὶ ἀβρώτων πρότερον, ἥδιστα νῦν γέγονεν, ὥσπερ οἰνόμελι, καὶ μήτρα· [Polla gar tōn ageustōn kai abrōtōn proteron, hēdista nyn gegonen, hōsper oinomeli, kai mētra] For many things which were formerly not tasted or eaten are now held to be most delicious, such as mead and sow's womb. Or is it because the gluttony of later times added so much to the inventions of the ancients that the thing could be considered new? Thus not even the name οἰνόμελι [oinomeli] occurs anywhere, so far as I know, before Dioscorides. And in the passage of Nehemiah cited above, the Hebrew has only שתו ממתקים, Drink sweet things, and the Greek version Πίετε γλυκάσματα [Piete glykasmata]. So also 3 Ezra 9:52.

The medicinal use of honey has already ^{x)} been treated, on those words of the Greek version about the bee, Proverb. VI, 8. Ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς τε καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται [Hēs tous ponous basileis te kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai], Whose labours (that is, honey) kings and private persons use for health. Add to these the passage on Jonathan, 1 Sam 14:27: Stretching out the tip of the rod which he had in his hand, he dipped it in a honeycomb; and when he had put his hand to his mouth, his eyes regained their light. The Arabic adds لان كان اظلم [III, 391] عليه [li-an kāna aẓlama ʿalayhi] Because darkness had come over him. That is, through hunger, as with Plautus' Curculio, [col. 527] who, pressed by hunger, bursts out in these words, Act 2, Scene 3:
— darkness comes over me, my knees give way from hunger.
And a little later,
— — — I am done for, I can hardly see, my mouth is bitter, my teeth clogged, my throat bleary with hunger.

To have one's sight darkened by hunger is said in Arabic اسدف [asdafa] asdapha, a most proper verb. Further, as the distinguished Vossius rightly observes on this passage, book 4 On Idolatry, ch. 79, while all food has the property of restoring lost strength, honey, like wine, does this especially, because both are subtle and therefore diffuse their power more quickly. Some observe that it is a property of honey to dispel dimness of the eyes. Many ancients assert this: Dioscorides, book 2, on honey: Ἀποκαθαίρει δὲ τὰ ἐπισκοτοῦντα ταῖς κόραις· [Apokathairei de ta episkotounta tais korais] It cleanses away what brings dimness on the eyes. Pliny, book 29, ch. 6: Honey in which bees have died is most useful for the eyes. Serenus Sammonicus [=Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, Liber medicinalis], ch. 14:
The juices of Hyblaean honey with goat's gall help eyes oppressed by dreadful darkness.

But these things are adduced in vain, since we read that honey benefits the eyes not by being eaten but by being smeared on them. I cannot wonder enough why Jerome, in the Epistle to Fabiola on the 42 stations, thinks that by the name of honey, which Jonathan tasted, a harlot is signified: "Honey," he says, "drips from the lips of a harlot woman: of which I think, according to the mystical senses, Jonathan tasted, and, being perhaps caught, was scarcely set free by the prayers of the people."

To the medical uses of honey the masters also refer the fact that in Isa 30:6 the camel's hump is called in Hebrew דבשת dabbeseth, as if from the word דבש debas, which means honey. It would be so called, as it were, because when it has been injured by burdens it is customarily anointed with honey. R. Selomo on Isaiah: על שם שמתרקבת תמיד וסכין שם דבש לרפואה קרויה דבשת, "Because it is always festering, and they anoint it with honey to heal it, it is called dabbeseth." The Talmudists assert the same in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 8 and 14, and in Bava Metsia, ch. 3. I do not agree, however, because this derivation seems far-fetched. The Arabic سديف [sadīf] sadinh, of the same meaning, alludes in some way to the Hebrew דבשת. For perhaps from דבשת dabbeseth was first made دفيس [dafīs] daphis, then by metathesis سديف [sadīf] sadiph; let the experts judge ^{R10}.

[III, 392] On the use of honey for laying out and embalming corpses I find nothing in Scripture. Unless someone thinks it was employed by the Egyptian physicians who embalmed Jacob: for in Egypt this was done. Hence Statius in the Propempticon for Metius Celer:
"Lead on also to the Emathian shades, where the warlike founder of the city endures, steeped in Hyblaean nectar."

That is, to the city of Alexandria, where the body of its founder Alexander is preserved, steeped in honey. And in Eutychius of Alexandria, Philemon, when about to carry that same corpse to Alexandria, ملاه عسلا [malāhu ʿasalan], filled it with honey. And Pliny, book 7, ch. 3, on Claudius Caesar: "We saw, during his principate, one brought to him from Egypt in honey" (a hippocentaur). This rite was also practised by the Babylonians, of whom Herodotus says in book 1: ταφαὶ δέ σφι ἐν μέλιτι [taphai de sphi en meliti]. And by the Lacedaemonians, when kings who had died abroad were to be brought home. Thus Agesipolis, when he had died at Aphytis in Macedonia, ἐν μέλιτι τιθεὶς, καὶ κομισθεὶς οἴκαδε, ἔτυχε τῆς βασιλικῆς ταφῆς [en meliti titheis, kai komistheis oikade, etyche tēs basilikēs taphēs], "placed in honey and brought home, received a royal burial." So Xenophon, book 1 of the Hellenica. And his colleague in the kingship, Agesilaus, when he had fallen ill and died at the harbour of Menelaus between Egypt and Cyrene, [col. 528] τοῦ σώματος ἐν μέλιτι κομισθέντος εἰς τὴν Σπάρτην, ἔτυχε τῆς βασιλικῆς ταφῆς τε, καὶ τιμῆς [tou sōmatos en meliti komisthentos eis tēn Spartēn, etyche tēs basilikēs taphēs te, kai timēs], "his body, carried in honey to Sparta, received royal burial and honour." These are the words of Diodorus, Histories, book 15. Yet Plutarch writes in his Life that, for lack of honey, he was embalmed in wax. To the same custom these lines of Lucretius, book 3, verse 902, allude:

"For if in death it is an evil to be mauled by the jaws and bites of wild beasts, I do not find why it is not bitter to be laid on fires and to be scorched by hot flames, or, placed in honey, to be suffocated," etc.

And Corippus too, in book 3, describing the funeral of Justinian, teaches in these words that among the most excellent aromatics, namely incense and balsam, with which the bodies of emperors were embalmed, honey also had a place:

"They burn Sabaean incense; they pour fragrant honey into the bowls set out, and balsam with its scented juice; a hundred other spices and wondrous ointments are brought, preserving the sacred body for all time."

For Pliny writes, book 22, ch. 24, that the nature of honey is such "that it does not allow bodies to putrefy, with a pleasant and not harsh taste, a nature other than that of salt." And Democritus wanted bodies to be preserved in honey in hope of resurrection. This I have learned from two passages of the ancients. One is of Varro, in Nonius, ch. 3, under the word Vulgus: [III, 393] "Heraclides Ponticus was wiser, who directed that they should burn them, than Democritus, who directed that they should preserve them in honey." The other is of Pliny, book 7, ch. 55: "Similar too is the vanity promised by Democritus about preserving human bodies and bringing them back to life, who did not come back to life himself."

The law concerning honey is found in Lev 2:11–12. No leaven and no honey shall you burn to God as an offering to be consumed by fire. As an offering of first fruits, however, you shall offer them to the Lord. But they shall not be offered upon the altar for a sweet savour. Here R. Selomo understands by the name of honey כל מתיקת פרי, all the sweetness of fruits, and some in Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] understand dates, as in 2 Chr 31:5, where the Israelites are said to have offered the first fruits of grain, must, oil and honey, and all the produce of the field. And indeed it will seem probable that Ezra means the same thing as is meant in the Law, since both passages deal with the first fruits of honey offered, or to be offered, to God. But if the Law were speaking of dates, or of the fruits of trees in general, the Law would nowhere have forbidden the use of honey in sacrifices. Yet all the ancients consistently teach that it was forbidden: among outside writers, Plutarch, book 4 of the Symposiaca, ch. 5; among the Jews, Philo, Περὶ θυόντων [Peri thyontōn]; from the choir of the Fathers, Jerome, Chrysostom, Procopius, Cyril, Theodoret, etc. So, whatever the more recent Hebrews may hold, I think that in both places the name דבש signifies honey, and that what is first gathered from the hives in springtime is called the first fruits of honey. Further, why the Law forbids honey to be offered on the altar, no one can easily say, and different people devise different reasons. Philo says honey is forbidden ἐπειδήπερ ἡ συναγωγὸς αὐτοῦ μέλιττα ζῶόν ἐστιν οὐ καθαρὸν, σήψεως καὶ φθορᾶς νεκρῶν, ὡς ὁ λόγος, βοῶν γεννώμενον [epeidēper hē synagōgos autou melitta zōon estin ou katharon, sēpseōs kai phthoras nekrōn, hōs ho logos, boōn gennōmenon], because its gatherer, the bee, is an impure animal, which they say is born from the putrefaction and corruption of dead oxen. Others, in Theodoret, say ὡς τῆς μελίττης καὶ ἀκαθάρτοις τόποις ἐφιζανούσης, καὶ πάντοθεν ἀθροιζούσης τῆς μελιττουργίας τὰς ἀφορμὰς [hōs tēs melittēs kai akathartois topois ephizanousēs, kai pantothen athroizousēs tēs melittourgias tas aphormas], because the bee settles in impure places and gathers the material for making honey from everywhere. Others, in the same author, say διδάσκεσθαι ἡμᾶς ἐξ οἰκείων πόνων τὰς θυσίας ἐπιτελεῖν, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Σολομῶντος παραίνεσιν· ὁ δὲ τῆς μελίττης καρπὸς, οὐχ ἡμέτερός φασι πόνος [didaskesthai hēmas ex oikeiōn ponōn tas thysias epitelein, kata tēn tou Solomōntos parainesin; ho de tēs melittēs karpos, ouch hēmeteros phasi ponos], that we are taught by this that sacrifices must be paid from our own labours; but the fruit of the bee, as they say, does not come from our labour. He himself thinks that διὰ τοῦ μέλιτος τὴν ἡδονὴν ἀπαγορεύεσθαι [dia tou melitos tēn hēdonēn apagoreuesthai], under the name of honey pleasure is forbidden. This you may also read in Philo. And Jerome, in the ninth letter, to Eustochium, says that honey is not offered in the sacrifices of God, because with God nothing voluptuous, [col. 529] nothing merely sweet, is pleasing, unless it contains something of biting truth. And in the twelfth letter, to Gaudentius, to teach that one must abstain from the allurements of the flesh, he says: In the sacrifices of the Lord they do not offer honey; and, wax being despised, which is the lodging of honey, oil is lit in the temple of God, which is pressed out of the bitterness of olives. And Isychius on this passage wants it to be understood as the doctrine of the pagans, on account of the sweetness of their words and the charm of their eloquence. These views, though rather uncertain, can be [III, 394] tolerated. But it is laughable that Plutarch, while trying to prove that the Jews worshipped Bacchus, adduces among other things this, in book 4 of the Symposiaca, question 5: Ἔτι τοίνυν μέλι μὲν οὐ προσφέρουσι ταῖς ἱερουργίαις, ὅτι δοκεῖ φθείρειν τὸν οἶνον κεραννύμενον [Eti toinyn meli men ou prospherousi tais hierourgiais, hoti dokei phtheirein ton oinon kerannymenon]· Further, they do not offer honey in sacrifices, because when mixed with wine it seems to spoil it. As if they feared to provoke Bacchus by tainting wine with a mixture of honey. This reason is most absurd. For they could have offered wine and honey to Bacchus separately. Nor did this scruple affect the true worshippers of Bacchus, who offered him not only wine but also honey. The matter is certain from Tibullus, who addresses Bacchus thus in book 1, Elegy 8:
So may you come today: to you I would give the honours of incense, and bring cakes sweet with Mopsopian honey.
Ovid agrees, book 3 of the Fasti, verse 735:
Cakes are made for the god, because he delights in sweet juices, and they say honey was discovered by Bacchus.

Hence his name Brisaeus, as we noted above. But that honey was also commonly offered to other gods, there is no one who does not know. This God reproaches the Jewish congregation with in chapter 16 of Ezekiel: You made for yourself male images, he says, to play the harlot with them, etc. And my food which I had given you, fine flour, and oil, and honey, with which I had fed you, this you offered to them for a sweet savour. For there was hardly any of the gods to whom libation was not made with honey. Thus Antipater of Sidon says of Mercury, book 1 of the Anthology, chapter 38:
Εὔκολος Ἑρμείας, ὦ ποιμένες, ἐν δὲ γάλακτι Χαίρων, καὶ δρυΐνῳ σπενδόμενος μέλιτι· [Eukolos Hermeias, ō poimenes, en de galakti Chairōn, kai dryinō spendomenos meliti]
Easy to please is Mercury, O shepherds, who delights in milk and is appeased with oak honey. And Silius of Pluto, book 13, verse 415:
Bring with you the foretold appeasements for the sacred rites of harsh Dis, honey too, and carry the gifts of pure Lyaeus.
And Apollonius of Hecate, book 3 of the Argonautica, verse 1034.
Μουνογενῆ δ' Ἑκάτην Περσηΐδα μειλίσσοιο Λείβων ἐκ δέπαος σιμβλήϊα ἔργα μελισσῶν· [Mounogenē d' Hekatēn Persēida meilissoio Leibōn ek depaos simblēia erga melissōn]

Appease the only-begotten Hecate, daughter of Perses, pouring from a bowl the works of the bees that are made in the hives. And of Priapus the shepherd Astacus says in the second Eclogue of Calpurnius,
And we give dripping honeycombs and flowing honey.
Likewise it was the custom to offer honey to Janus together with little dates and figs, so that the year might be sweeter; Ovid, Fasti book 1, line 185:

[III, 395] What is the meaning of the date, and the wrinkled dried fig, I said, and the white honey given in a snow-white jar? It is for the omen, he said, that this flavour may follow events, and that the year may complete the course it has begun-
An oracle of Apollo in Eusebius, book 4 of the Praeparatio Evangelica, also commands that honey and wine be set before the Nymphs:
Χεῦε μέλι νύμφαισι, Διωνύσοιό τε δῶρα, [Cheue meli nymphaisi, Diōnysoio te dōra]
Pour honey for the Nymphs, and the gifts of Bacchus. But the Furies too are appeased with honey in Silius, in the place cited above:
Then to you, Alecto, and to you, never joyful Megaera, the chosen bodies of woolly two-year-old sheep fall down; they pour honey over them, and the tribute of Bacchus and of milk.

But to show once and for all that there was no god who was not believed to delight in honey, one should read Pausanias in the First Book of Elis. There, after listing at least fifty altars erected to various deities in the temple of Olympian Zeus, some of them in that list sacred to all the gods, he says: Ἑκάστου δὲ ἅπαξ τοῦ μηνὸς θύουσιν ἐπὶ πάντων Ἠλεῖοι τῶν κατειλεγμένων βωμῶν, θύουσι δὲ ἀρ- [col. 530] χαῖόν τινα τρόπον· λιβανωτὸν γὰρ ὁμοῦ πυροῖς μεμιγμένοις μέλιτι θυμιῶσιν ἐπὶ τὸν βωμόν [Hekastou de hapax tou mēnos thyousin epi pantōn Ēleioi tōn kateilegmenōn bōmōn, thyousi de archaion tina tropon; libanōton gar homou pyrois memigmenois meliti thymiōsin epi ton bōmon]. Once every month the Eleans sacrifice at all the altars we have listed, by a certain ancient rite, burning frankincense together with wheat kneaded with honey. Strabo, book 15, also describes the Persians in all their sacrifices as ἀποσπένδοντας ἔλαιον, ὁμοῦ γάλακτι καὶ μέλιτι κεκραμένον [apospendontas elaion, homou galakti kai meliti kekramenon], pouring libations of oil mixed with milk and honey. Accordingly Homer, or whoever it is, in the Hymn to Hermes, calls honey
— — — Θεῶν ἡδεῖαν ἐδωδὴν, [Theōn hēdeian edōdēn]

the sweet food of the gods. And the mouse in the Batrachomyomachia, boastfully listing his delicacies to the frog, says: I do not lack thrice-kneaded bread, nor cake seasoned with sesame, nor slices of ham, nor livers, nor cheese,
Οὐ χρηστὸν μελίτωμα, τὸ καὶ μάκαρες ποθέουσιν, [Ou chrēston melitōma, to kai makares potheousin]

nor the excellent honey sweetmeat which even the gods desire. Sacrifices of this kind Plutarch calls νηφάλια, καὶ μελίσπονδα [nēphalia, kai melisponda] in the book On Restraining Anger, and in the Symposiaca, book 4, question 5. I pass over the frequent use of honey among funeral offerings and libations for the dead. Thus Achilles at the funeral of Patroclus, Iliad ψ′ [psi]:
Ἐν δὲ τίθει μέλιτος καὶ ἀλείφατος ἀμφιφορῆας, [En de tithei melitos kai aleiphatos amphiphorēas]

He placed (on the bier) jars of honey and oil. And in Odyssey ώ [ō] the body of Achilles is burned, [III, 396] — — ἐντ᾽ ἐσθῆτι θεῶν, καὶ ἀλείφατι πολλῷ, Καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ, — — — [ent' esthēti theōn, kai aleiphati pollō, Kai meliti glykerō]
in the garment of the gods, and with much oil and sweet honey. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris prepares funeral offerings for her brother Orestes:
Πηγὰς τ᾽ οὐρείων ἐκ μόσχων Βάκχου τ᾽ οἰνηρὰς λοιβὰς, Ξουθᾶν τε πόνημα μελισσᾶν, [Pēgas t' oureiōn ek moschōn Bakchou t' oinēras loibas, Xouthan te ponēma melissan]
Streams of blood from mountain calves, and the winy libation of Bacchus, and the labour of the tawny bees. So it reads at line 163. And again, addressing him as one about to die, at line 632:

Πολύν τε γάρ σοι κόσμον ἐνθήσω τάφῳ, Καὶ τῆς ὀρείας ἀνθεμόῤῥυτον γάνος Ξουθῆς μελίσσης εἰς πῦρ ἐμβαλῶ σέθεν, [Polyn te gar soi kosmon enthēsō taphō, Kai tēs oreias anthemorrhyton ganos Xouthēs melissēs eis pyr embalō sethen]
For I will place much adornment for you in the tomb, and I will cast onto your pyre the delights of the tawny mountain bee, flowing from the flowers. I likewise pass over
the cake drugged with honey and medicated grain,

thrown to Cerberus by Aeneas. Here I do not approve of the reading saporatam [flavoured], for which a man easily the most learned of his age ^{y)} contends with so much effort. For although Tertullian, Arnobius, Marcellinus and other writers of a later age said saporatum for conditum [seasoned], yet in the age of Augustus the word was entirely unknown and used by no one. And although that excellent man flatly denies that honey has any power to induce sleep, Coelius Rhodiginus ^{z)} proves from Orpheus that the ancients thought otherwise: Orpheus relates that Saturn was ensnared by Jupiter through his craving for honey and lulled to sleep. To this I add these words of Iamblichus in Photius, author 94: Οἱ δὲ τῷ μέλιτι καρωθέντες μόλις ἀνίστανται [Hoi de tō meliti karōthentes molis anistantai]. But those stupefied by honey scarcely wake up. But this is more than enough about honey. I add only that God, for the very reason that honey was used almost constantly in the rites of demons, regarded it as impure and did not want it offered in his own sacrifices ^{R11}.
[III, 397] Another product of the bee is wax, no less useful than honey. For from wax are made tapers, by which darkness is put to flight. Martial:
This taper will furnish you with fires by night.
It also serves as glue. Virgil:
Pan first taught to join several reeds with wax. — — — — —

Corpses were embalmed with wax no less than with honey. Thus Herodotus in book 4 reports that the Scythians carried the body of a dead king, κατακεκηρωμένον [katakekērōmenon], throughout all Scythia before burying it. And in book 1 the same author says of the Persians: κατακηρώσαντες τὸν νεκρὸν γῇ κρύπτουσι [katakērōsantes ton nekron gē kryptousi]. Hence Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book 1: the Persians embalm them after coating them with wax, so that the bodies may last as long as possible. And [col. 531] Strabo, book 15: Θάπτουσι δὲ κηρῷ περιπλάσσοντες τὰ σώματα [Thaptousi de kērō periplassontes ta sōmata]. So the well-known word موميا [mūmiyā] mumia seems to be derived from موم [mūm] mum. So the Persians call wax, and the Arabs call προπόλιν [propolin]. And the words of Isaiah, chapter 64, verse 2, כקדוח אש המסים מים, the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint] render thus: Ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ προσώπου πυρὸς τήκεται [Hōs kēros apo prosōpou pyros tēketai]. For in place of מים, that is, waters, they read מום, that is, wax; and כקדם אש, as before fire, in place of כקדוח אש, as fire burns. So already at that time the word מום mum was in use for wax, whence mumia. Wax was also much used in writing, in writing tablets, in painting, in cosmetics, and in seals, a use that lasts to this day. But these matters belong elsewhere.

The sacred writers often compare things with wax melting before fire. Thus David, Ps 22:15: My heart is like wax, it melts within me. And Ps 68:3: As wax melts before fire, so the wicked perish before God. And Ps 97:5: The mountains melt like wax before the Lord. And Mic 1:4: The mountains shall melt under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, like wax before the fire. Hence the writer of the book of Judith, whoever he is, chapter 16, verse 18: The rocks [III, 398] shall melt like wax at your presence. So too the profane authors everywhere. Theocritus in the Pharmaceutria:
Ὡς τοῦτον τὸν καρὸν ἐγὼ, σὺν δαίμονι, τάκω, [Hōs touton ton karon egō, syn daimoni, takō,] Ὡς τάκοιθ᾽ ὑπ᾽ ἔρωτος ὁ Μύνδιος αὐτίκα Δέλφις. [Hōs takoith᾽ hyp᾽ erōtos ho Myndios autika Delphis.]
As I, with the god's help, melt this wax, so may Delphis of Myndus at once melt with love. Hence Virgil:
As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts in one and the same fire, so may Daphnis with love of me.
Lucretius on clouds, book 6, verse 512:

Moreover, when the clouds too are thinned by the winds, or are dissolved when struck from above by the heat of the sun, they let fall rainy moisture, dripping, as when wax wasting over a hot fire melts abundantly.
Ovid on Narcissus, book 3 of the Metamorphoses:
He could bear it no longer, but as yellow wax wastes in a gentle fire, and morning frost in the sun, so, worn away by love, he melts and is slowly consumed by a hidden fire.
And in book 10, on the statue of Pygmalion:
It yielded under his fingers and gave way, as Hymettian wax softens in the sun. — — — —
Lucan on Sabellus, who had been bitten by the seps serpent, book 9, verse 783:
— — his shoulders melt, and his strong arms; his neck and head flow away; not faster does snow dissolve and fall before the warm South Wind, nor will wax yield to the sun.
Asclepiades, Anthology book 7, Epigram 26:
Τήκομαι ὡς κηρὸς παρ᾽ πυρὶ, κάλλος ὁρῶν· [Tēkomai hōs kēros par᾽ pyri, kallos horōn;]
I melt like wax at the fire, beholding beauty.

Wax is called in Hebrew דונג, but in Chaldee שעוה; hence the Hebrew verb השתעה means to soften like wax, if we believe the masters, who render these words of Isa 41:10, אל תשתע כי אני אלהיך, roughly in this sense: Do not soften (like wax), for I am your God. So R. Selomo. And Kimchi observes that his forebears interpreted it thus, namely in Bereshit Rabba, section 65, in these words: כיון שאמר [III, 399] יצחק ליעקוב גשה נא ואמשוכך בני נשפכו מים על שוקיו והיה לבו רפה כשעוה וזמן לו הקדוש ברוך הוא שני מלאכים אחד בימינו ואחד בשמאלו והיו אוחזין אותו במרפקו כדי שלא יפול הדא הוא דכתיב אל תשתע כי אני אלהיך, When Isaac said to Jacob (who was hiding under Esau's garment to obtain the blessing), Genes. XXVII, 21. „Come near, I pray, my son, that I may touch you“: his legs ran with sweat, [col. 532] and his heart softened like wax. But God, holy and blessed, prepared for him two angels, one on his right, the other on his left, to hold him under the arm so that he would not fall. Hence what is said in Isa 41:10 „Do not soften (like wax), for I am your God.“

The word נכאת necoth, of very uncertain meaning, in Genes. XXXVII, 25. and XLIII, 11., is explained by Jonathan as שעוא and by Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] as شمعا [shamʿan], that is, wax, as also by the author of Beresith Rabba, section 91, near the end. And in Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] they think that שעך is the very same thing, because it comes close to שעוא. However that may be, other interpreters explain it very differently. The LXX have θυμίαμα [thymiama] or θυμιάματα [thymiamata]; Aquila, στύρακα [styraka]; Jerome in the first passage aromata [spices], in the second storacem [storax], like Aquila; the Syriac ܪ̈ܗܛܢܐ [רהטנא], resin; the Samaritan ࠒࠈࠐ [קטף], balsam; the Arabic version published at Paris, خرنوبا [kharnūban], just as some in Kimchi have חרוב, carob; two Arabic manuscripts in Sweden صمغا [ṣamghan], gum; Rabbi Moses the Priest and Kimchi, דבר נחמד, a desirable thing; R. Selomo, כנוסי בשמים הרבה, collections of many spices. In this doubtful matter the later writers follow one or another of the older ones, as seemed good to them. Junius alone, taking a path of his own, rendered it myxaria [sebesten plums], which, he says, are called in Arabic NUKETA, according to Aegineta, Aëtius, Psellus and Actuarius, a word very close to the Hebrew NEKOTH. But this man, otherwise pious and learned, has missed the point. For the Arabic name of the sebesten, مخيط [mukhayṭ] mucchait, as the Arabs consistently write it, has not a single letter in common with the Hebrew נכאת nechoth, as anyone who is not entirely ἀναλφάβητος [analphabētos] in these languages will at once recognize. Nor do the authors he cites mention the Arabic name; among the Greeks only Charito, as far as I know, does so, writing μουχαῖτας [mouchaitas], as the apothecaries write mukeitas and mokaitas. Most of the other more recent writers explain נכאת necoth as θυμιάματα [thymiamata], spices, with the Greeks, Jerome and some of the Hebrews. That this can hardly stand will be evident to anyone who reads the two passages of Scripture in which this word occurs. The first reads thus, Gen 37:25. Lifting up their eyes they saw; and behold, a company of Ishmaelite travellers coming from Gilead, whose camels were carrying נכאת nechoth, and resin, and stacte; and they were going to carry them down into Egypt. And the second, Gen 43:11. Take of the most praised fruits of this land in your vessels, to carry a gift to that man, a little resin, נכאת nechoth, and stacte, and pistachios, and almonds. From reading these the attentive reader will see that נכאת is not θυμιάματα [thymiamata], or spices, or a desirable thing [III, 400] in general, but something particular, like honey, resin, stacte, etc., which are mentioned in the same place. And I have several reasons why Aquila, who rendered it storax, pleases me most. Let the first be this: that storax grows abundantly in Syria. Pliny, book 12, chapter 25: Syria, next to Judaea, above Phoenicia, produces storax around Gabala and Marathus, and Casius, the mountain of Seleucia. Dioscorides, book 2, after giving the marks of the best storax, says Τοιοῦτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ Καταβαλίτης, καὶ Πισσιδιακὸς, καὶ Κιλίκιος [Toioutos de estin ho Katabalitēs, kai Pissidiakos, kai Kilikios], where for ὁ Καταβαλίτης [ho Katabalitēs] one should read ὁ Γαβαλίτης [ho Gabalitēs], that is, from the very well-known city of Syria, Gabala, which Pliny mentions. Others assign it to Phoenicia, like Artemidorus in Stephanus under Κάρνη [Karnē]. And Josephus to Galilee, Antiquities book 15, chapter 23. Second, storax is rightly counted among the most praised fruits of the land, since physicians particularly commend its use among the spices. Third, as here the Ishmaelites, so in Pliny, book 12, chapter 17, the Arabs bring back storax from Syria. Fourth, it is not without reason that Moses joins storax with resin, [col. 533] honey and stacte of myrrh, since it approaches their nature. Accordingly Dioscorides describes the best storax as ῥητινώδης [rhētinōdēs], resinous, καὶ ἐν τῷ μαλάσσεσθαι ἀνεὶς ὑγρασίαν τινὰ μελιτώδη [kai en tō malassesthai aneis hygrasian tina melitōdē], and when kneaded giving off a honey-like liquid. And to it is attributed δάκρυον κόμμι ἐοικὸς, διαυγὲς, σμηρνίζον [dakryon kommi eoikos, diauges, smērnizon], a tear like gum, translucent, like myrrh. So also Isidore, book 17, chapter 8: Storax calamites, fat, resinous, of a pleasant smell, moist, and as it were giving off a honeyed liquid. Hence in Pliny storax is adulterated with cedar resin, or gum, at other times with honey. Fifth, I think I can detect the origin of the Hebrew name, hitherto unknown. The Arabic verb نكت [nakata] nachatha means 1. to strike the ground with a spear so that a mark remains impressed; 2. to throw someone pierced by a spear on his head; and النكت [al-nakt] is such a piercing, and النكات [al-nakkāt] one who pierces thus. Why should the Hebrew name of storax, נכאת nechoth, not allude to this, since from the storax tree are made τὰ στυράκινα ἀκοντίσματα ἐοικότα τοῖς κρανεΐνοις [ta styrakina akontismata eoikota tois kraneinois], storax javelins similar to those made of cornel? So it is in Strabo, book 12. And accordingly in the Greek Hesychius σύραξ [syrax] means not only storax, the tree or the spice, but also a lance, and a part of the spear, either the lowest or the highest. For the ancients do not agree well on this. In Pollux, book 1, chapter 10: Τὸ μὲν τέλος τοῦ δόρατος σαυρωτὴρ, τὸ δὲ προῦχον αἰχμὴ, καὶ ἐπιδορατὶς, καὶ στύραξ [To men telos tou doratos saurōtēr, to de prouchon aichmē, kai epidoratis, kai styrax], the lowest part of the spear is the sauroter, and the top the point, and the styrax. Yet in the same author, book 10, chapter 31, σαυρωτὴρ [saurōtēr] and στύραξ [styrax] are the same. So also in Hesychius, Suidas and the Etymologicum. And in Athenaeus, book 12, Heraclides of Cyme describes the μηλοφόροι [mēlophoroi] of the Persians, the melophori, ἐπὶ τῶν συράκων μῆλα χρυσᾶ ἔχοντες [epi tōn syrakōn mēla chrysa echontes], having golden apples on their styraces (that is, on the tops of their spear-shafts). And this is precisely the στυράκιον [styrakion] in book 2 of Thucydides, where we read that a certain Plataean shut the gates of the city στυρακίῳ ἀντὶ [styrakiō anti] [III, 401] βαλάνου χρησάμενος ἐς τὸν μοχλὸν [balanou chrēsamenos es ton mochlon], driving the butt of a spear-shaft into the bar instead of a bolt-pin. And the verb συρακίζειν [syrakizein] in Hesychius is κεντρίζειν [kentrizein], to prick, as with a spear or the point of a spear. Sixth, if we contend by authority, Aquila, for whom נכאת nechoth is σύραξ [syrax], is followed by Jerome at Gen 43:11, where he renders storax. And in the Book of Names you may read NECHOTA, storax, or spices. I suspect that the Syrians, who explained it as resin, and the Arabs, who explained it as gum, held the same view, but misused a generic name because the specific one was unknown to them. With נכאת nechoth, the spice, the Hebrews wrongly confuse נכותה necotha, which is plainly something else, Isa 39:2 and 2 Reg. XX, 13., as will be said elsewhere ^{R12}.

notes.text: For example the syrup made from raisins, which the Arabs still today call دِبْس [dibs]; even in our own age so much of it is sent every year from the region of Hebron to Egypt as three hundred camels can carry, as Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] writes in his Travels, p. 293 of the German version, note. Of this syrup [III, 375] Russell [=Alexander Russell, The Natural History of Aleppo (1756)], in the Natural History of Aleppo, p. 20: the juice of the Grapes is sometimes thikened in a substance, that hath the appearance of a coarse honey, and is called Dibbs. Itis brought to markets in skins, has a sweet taste, and is much used by the people of all rank. Kaempfer in Amoenitt. exott. fasc. 2, p. 380: A large part of the grapes is reduced by boiling to a syrup, which takes the place of butter on the tables of the poor and, mixed with water, serves those who abstain from wine in place of wine. Olearius [=Adam Olearius, travels in Persia] in der Persianischen und Moscowitischen Reisebeschreibung book 5, ch. 9, p. 577: Aus dem Moste machen die Perser einen Syrup, welchen sie Duschab nennen. Sie kochen den Most so lange, bis nur der sechste Theil davon übrig bleibt, und wie ein dickes Oel fliesst. Wenn er gebraucht werden soll, wird er mit Wasser und ein wenig Essig vermischt, welches sodann ein angenehmes Getränke giebt. Sie kochen auch bisweilen den Duschab so hart, dass man ihn schneiden kann. Die Reisenden pflegen ihn so trokken mitzunehmen, und im Wasser in ihrem Getränke zu zerlassen. Cf. below, note 8.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: Similarly Suidas, under the word ἀκρίδας [akridas]: ἤσθιε δε ἀκριδας ὁ προδρομος καὶ μελι ἀγριον, ὁπερ ἀπο των δενδρων ἐπισυναγομενον μαννα τοις πολλοις προσαγορευεται· [ēsthie de akridas ho prodromos kai meli agrion, hoper apo tōn dendrōn episynagomenon manna tois pollois prosagoreuetai] the forerunner ate ἀκριδας [akridas] and wild honey, which is gathered from trees and is commonly called manna. This view was also adopted by Wesseling on Diodor. Sic. Bibl. book 19, §94, by Reland [=Adriaan Reland, Dissertationes miscellaneae (1706–08)] in Palaestina, book 1, ch. 54, p. 382, and by Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes], whose words in the Commentatio de Manna (at the end of the Exercitationes de homonymis hyles iatricae, Utrecht 1689, folio), p. 254, are these: But that wild honey, on which in
notes.label: R3

notes.text: But J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] Hebrr. vol. 4, p. 1134, contends that יער and יערה are honey dripping from trees, which Diodorus Siculus, Biblioth. book 19, §94, calls μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. He is moved chiefly by this argument: in 1 Sam 14:27 (var. 25. 26.) the Israelites, pursuing the Philistines through a forest, are said to have come upon a large tract covered with honey, whereas bees' honey certainly does not cover wide estates. He adds that in v. 27 Jonathan is said to have dipped his staff ביערת הדבש, and that it is not credible that someone who had disturbed with a staff the honey stores of bees placed on the ground would have gone unpunished. But it is nowhere said that a large tract was covered with honey; in verse 25 we read only these words: ויהי דבש על-פני השדה, honey was found on the ground, which had flowed down from hollows of trees or from clefts in rocks (cf. below, notes 5, 6). Into this honey lying on the ground Jonathan could dip his staff with impunity. — Much less acceptable is the opinion of Rabbi Nathan the Ishmaelite, who interprets יערת דבש as forest of honey, understanding by that name a thicket of sugar canes; this opinion was followed by R. Solomon Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists], and after him defended by Cocceius and Gussetius in their Lexicons and by Hiller in Hierophyt. vol. 2, p. 203–204. But Michaelis rightly observes, in the Supplemm. p. 1135, that this meaning fits neither 1 Sam 14:27 nor Song 5:1 "There are sugar canes in Eretz Yisrael, I admit, but in the place where the battle with the Philistines was fought there were no thickets of sugar canes or of other reeds, much less such large ones that a victorious people pursuing the vanquished could have entered them. Further, and this alone is enough, who, travelling through sugar canes, could dip a staff into them and bring honey extracted from them to his mouth?" — Let the meaning honeycomb stand, then, which the passage Song 5:1 virtually demands: I have eaten יַעְרִי עִם דִּבְשִׁי, my honeycomb with my honey, as the Vulgate translator has it. Cf. also Velthusen's [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses] commentary on this passage of the Song, p. 392.

notes.text: In this passage, however, Michaelis, in the Supplemm. vol. 2, p. 391 f., contends that honey made from raisins (on which see note 1 above) is to be understood. "Bees' honey," he says, "cannot possibly be meant. It would not only be a cheap gift, but all the more inept because it would be carrying owls to Athens; for Egypt abounds in honey, and indeed of the most excellent kind, having a spring and first harvest over two months. See Maillet's description of Egypt (description de l'Egypte, lettre neuvieme) p. 24, 25. Nor would anyone moderately acquainted with the nature of both regions think of palm honey; for Eretz Yisrael neither abounds in palms now nor ever greatly abounded in them, whereas Egypt is rich in them, and neighbouring Biledulgerid richer still, which even takes its name from the abundance of palms." Michaelis is followed by WARNEKROS in his treatise de fertilitate Palaestinae cum Aegypto comparata (in the Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat. vol. 15), §19, p. 221 ff. I doubt, however, whether in Jacob's time they knew how to boil syrup from raisins.

notes.text: But PETR. ADRIAN. VAN KOOTEN, in Observatt. ad nonnulla Canticor. loca (under the presidency of SEBALDUS RAVIUS, Utrecht, 1774), p. 16 ff., refers that comparison used by the Hebrew poet not to pleasant speech but to the saliva of the beloved, which the later Oriental poets are accustomed to compare with honey. Thus NUWEIRI (in REISKE on Tarafa, last page), listing the flowers of the Arab poets which they use in praising their beloveds, mentions this one among others: شبهوا اللما بالخمر والريق بالشهد [shabbahū al-lamā bi-l-khamr wa-l-rīq bi-l-shahd] they compare the gum to wine, the saliva to honey. And MUTANABBI (in the Excerpts published by Reiske, p. 43, verse 7), describing his beloved, says: مظلومة القد في تشبيهه غصنا [maẓlūmat al-qadd fī tashbīhihi ghuṣnan] مظلومة الريق في تشبيهه ضربا [maẓlūmat al-rīq fī tashbīhihi ḍaraban] Her stature is wronged if it is compared to a branch; her saliva is wronged if it is compared to honey. So too IMRU' AL-QAIS, in the Poem adorned with the prize, edited by Lette, verse 15, addresses his beloved thus: فقلت لها سيري وارخي زمامه [fa-qultu lahā sīrī wa-arkhī zimāmahu] ولا تبعدني من جناك المعسل [wa-lā tubʿidīnī min janāki al-muʿassal] I said to her: let him (the camel) go with slackened rein, and do not keep me from your most honeyed fruit. By the most honeyed fruit he means her saliva, or kisses that equal honey in sweetness. TOGHRAI uses the same figure where, imagining himself pierced and nearly slain by the spears, that is, the eyes, of his beloved, he says (verse 25): يشفي لديغ العولي في بيوتهم [yashfī ladīgh al-ʿawlī fī buyūtihim] بنهلة من غدير الخمر والعسل [bi-nahlatin min ghadīr al-khamr wa-l-ʿasal] He who is wounded by spears will be healed in their tents by even a single draught from a pool of wine and honey. These passages moved Michaelis, in the Biblioth. Orient et Exeget. vol. 7, p. 169 ff., to think that in that passage of the Song lascivious kisses are meant, such as the Florentine kiss (a kiss given with the tongue inserted into the other's mouth and licking the tongue). But Velthusen, in his commentary on the passage, p. 364, contends that the common interpretation, which understands that passage of pleasant and sweet speech, is to be retained, chiefly because of the parallel passages IV, 3. V, 16. II, 3. Prov 5:3.
