notes.text: "But if God had forbidden sacrifices to be made to him with honey only because it had found a place in the ceremonies of the gentiles, by the same reasoning he would also have placed among the forbidden things frankincense, salt and oil, which we find used in the rites of the gentiles from the earliest memory of pagan worship." This, in my judgement, is rightly urged against Bochart's opinion, which is also that of Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] (in the More Nebochim, vol. III, ch. 46), by SPENCER, de Legibus Hebraeorum Ritualibus, book 2, ch. 9, sect. 1, p. 280 f., ed. The Hague 1686, 4to. But much less satisfactory are the reasons he himself adduces for the prohibition of honey, the weightiest of which seems [III, 397] to be this one, which he also recommends in book 3, Dissert. 2, ch. 2, sect. 2, p. 140: "that God rejected honey and leaven from his altar at the same moment at which he ordered salt to be used, in order to signify tacitly that salt had been honoured by the usage of a purer antiquity, whereas honey and leaven (among many other things) had been devised recently and added to sacrifices for some reason drawn from the mysteries of profane theology. For when God gave the law, he seems to have aimed at freeing public worship from new rites that smacked of superstition, and at bringing it back to the simplicity received in the age of the patriarchs." Yet nearly the same is the opinion of SYKES, an Englishman, in the book he entitled an Essay on the nature, design and origin of Sacrifices, London 1746, p. 117 ff. of the German trans. (which appeared at Halle in 1778 with notes and a preface by J. S. Semler).
notes.label: R11

notes.text: Yet everyone will himself feel that the derivation of the word נכאת which Bochart gave is too far-fetched and therefore hardly probable. Nor is the opinion of LOUIS DE DIEU more satisfactory, who in his Animadversiones on Genes. XXXVII, 25. compares the Arabic نكيث [nakīth], which, as Firuzabadi teaches, is one of the سواك [siwāk], the name by which are designated all the dentifrices in daily use among the Arabs, among which certain aromatics are most esteemed, by which not only are the teeth cleaned but above all a fragrance is imparted to the breath of the mouth. But whether نكيث [nakīth] is rightly compared with the Hebrew נכאת, I doubt. Much less, however, does the interpretation of HILLER seem acceptable, who in the Hierophyt. vol. I, p. 212, renders נכאת as things pounded, crushed, from כתת, he pounded, so that נכאת would be written for נכתות, with א put in place of a repeated ת, just as ימאס, it will melt, is said for ימסס Job 7:5; שגיאה, error, for שגיגה, Ps 19:13; רבאות for רבובות, myriads, Esr. II, 69., after the manner of the Syrians, who for רגג say ראג, desiring, Gal. V, 17., and for רותת, with Thau changed into Aleph, ܪܬܝܬ [רתית], trembling, Acts 16:29. By the name of pounded things here he thinks pounded oils are to be understood, since in Exod 27:20. XXIX, 4. Lev 14:2 mention is made of שמן זית כתית, pounded olive oil, used for the lamps in the temple and for the sacred offerings. But in the Institt. Linguae Sanctae, p. 409, he understands by pounded things crushed aromatics, aromatic powders. However, not to mention that the examples Hiller adduces of א put in place of a repeated ת are very uncertain, since those words should rather be referred to different roots (for instance ימאס to מאס, שגיאה to שגא etc.), I also doubt that נכאת, if it truly means pounded things, was used absolutely for oils or pounded aromatics. Whoever wishes to know the much less probable conjectures of others may consult CLODIUS, Lexic. Hebr. Select. p. 339. To me the most satisfactory interpretation is the one Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] offered in the Clavis in Iesaiam, Chapter XXXIX, 2, p. 275 (although he rightly considers the נכתה occurring there to be different from our נכאת). He compares the Hebrew נכאת with the Arabic نَكَأَةٌ [nakaʾatun], which in GOLIUS is said to be the same as نُكَعَةٌ [nukaʿatun], the top of the طُرْثُوث [ṭurthūth], conspicuous for its reddish bark, resembling the flower of the amaranth, or its reddish flower, with which one is wont to dye. Also gum tragacanth: the latter meaning would fit the passages Genes. XXXVII, 25. XLIII, 11. exceedingly well.
